concepts: Equation of a line in 3D and a point at a given distance on it
questions.question: Let the point, on the line passing through the points $P(1,-2,3)$ and $Q(5,-4,7)$, farther from the origin and at a distance of 9 units from the point $P$, be $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$. Then $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: A point of the line at distance 9 from $P$ is $P\pm9\hat u$; the sign that moves away from the origin is the one asked for.
solution: The line $PQ$ has direction $(4,-2,4)$, so it is $\frac{x-1}{4}=\frac{y+2}{-2}=\frac{z-3}{4}$.
A general point of the line is $(4t+1,\,-2t-2,\,4t+3)$.
Its squared distance from $P$ is $16t^2+4t^2+16t^2=36t^2$, and this equals $81$.
For $t=\frac32$ the point is $(7,-5,9)$, at distance $\sqrt{155}$ from the origin; for $t=-\frac32$ it is $(-5,1,-3)$, at distance $\sqrt{35}$. The farther point is $(7,-5,9)$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes the squared distance as 16t^2+4t^2+16t^2 = 81 and jumps to t = +-3/2, then to the point (7,-5,9), without showing why t = +3/2 is the 'farther' point (the question asks for the farther one). Added the comparison of the two candidate points (7,-5,9) and (-5,1,-3); the answer 155 is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Walk 9 units along the unit direction $\hat u$ and use $|P+9\hat u|^2=|P|^2+81+18\,P\cdot\hat u$.
solution: The direction $\overrightarrow{PQ}=(4,-2,4)$ has length 6, so the unit direction is $\hat u=\frac13(2,-1,2)$.
$P\cdot\hat u=\frac13(2+2+6)=\frac{10}{3}>0$, so moving along $+\hat u$ takes us away from the origin: the farther point is $P+9\hat u$.
Without even finding the point: $|P+9\hat u|^2=|P|^2+81+18\,(P\cdot\hat u)=14+81+60=155$.

useful_results: Points at distance $d$ from $P$ along a line with unit direction $\hat u$ are $P\pm d\hat u$; the one farther from $O$ is $P+d\hat u$ whenever $P\cdot\hat u\ge0$.
$|P+d\hat u|^2=|P|^2+d^2+2d\,(P\cdot\hat u)$ gives the squared distance from the origin without finding coordinates.

Direction ratios of the line through $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2,z_2)$ are $(x_2-x_1,y_2-y_1,z_2-z_1)$; a parameter $t$ in $(x_1+at,\dots)$ gives distance $|t|\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}$ from the start point.

concepts: Line intersecting two given lines and parallel to a given line
questions.question: Let the line $L$ intersect the lines $x-2=-y=z-1$ and $2(x+1)=2(y-1)=z+1$ and be parallel to the line $\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y-1}{1}=\frac{z-2}{2}$. Then which of the following points lies on $L$?
questions.key_idea: Write a general point on each line; the join of the two points must be parallel to $(3,1,2)$.
solution: A general point of the first line is $(k+2,\,-k,\,k+1)$.
A general point of the second line is $\left(\frac{\alpha}{2}-1,\,\frac{\alpha}{2}+1,\,\alpha-1\right)$.
The join of these points is parallel to $(3,1,2)$: $\frac{\frac{\alpha}{2}-1-k-2}{3}=\frac{\frac{\alpha}{2}+1+k}{1}=\frac{\alpha-1-k-1}{2}$.
The first two ratios give $\alpha=-4k-6$; the last two give $\alpha+2+2k=\alpha-2-k$, so $3k=-4$.
So $L$ passes through $\left(\frac23,\frac43,-\frac13\right)$ and has direction $(3,1,2)$: $L:\frac{x-\frac23}{3}=\frac{y-\frac43}{1}=\frac{z+\frac13}{2}$.
The point $\left(-\frac13,1,-1\right)$ gives $\frac{-1}{3}=\frac{-1/3}{1}=\frac{-2/3}{2}=-\frac13$, so it lies on $L$: option (3).
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes the proportion for the join of the two points and then jumps straight to k = -4/3. Added the two linear equations that give k (alpha = -4k-6 and 3k = -4). No wrong value; the answer (3) is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Cut the second line with the plane through the first line parallel to $(3,1,2)$; that point and the direction fix $L$.
solution: The first line passes through $(2,0,1)$ with direction $(1,-1,1)$. The plane containing it and parallel to $(3,1,2)$ has normal $(1,-1,1)\times(3,1,2)=(-3,1,4)$.
Put the second line $\left(\frac{\alpha}{2}-1,\frac{\alpha}{2}+1,\alpha-1\right)$ in it: $-\frac{3\alpha}{2}+3+\frac{\alpha}{2}+1+4\alpha-4+2=3\alpha+2=0$, so $\alpha=-\frac23$.
The meeting point is $\left(-\frac43,\frac23,-\frac53\right)$; $L$ is the line through it with direction $(3,1,2)$ (the plane guarantees it meets the first line).
Test $\left(-\frac13,1,-1\right)$: difference from $\left(-\frac43,\frac23,-\frac53\right)$ is $\left(1,\frac13,\frac23\right)\parallel(3,1,2)$. It lies on $L$.

useful_results: The line meeting two skew lines $L_1,L_2$ and parallel to $\vec v$ is found by intersecting $L_2$ with the plane through $L_1$ parallel to $\vec v$ (normal $\vec d_1\times\vec v$), then drawing the parallel through that point.
The unknown parameters can be reduced by demanding the join $(\vec p_2-\vec p_1)\times\vec v=\vec 0$: two independent equations for two parameters.
A line is determined by one point and a direction: once one point of $L$ is known, any option is checked by testing parallelism of its difference vector with $\vec v$.

concepts: Scalar triple product and vector identities (cross-product equation)
questions.question: Let $\vec a=\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k$, $\vec b=3\left(\hat i-\hat j+\hat k\right)$. Let $\vec c$ be the vector such that $\vec a\times\vec c=\vec b$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec c=3$. Then $\vec a\cdot\left(\left(\vec c\times\vec b\right)-\vec b-\vec c\right)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $\vec a\cdot(\vec c\times\vec b)=(\vec a\times\vec c)\cdot\vec b=\vec b\cdot\vec b$, so no component of $\vec c$ is needed.
solution: $\vec a\cdot(\vec c\times\vec b)=[\vec a\ \vec c\ \vec b]=(\vec a\times\vec c)\cdot\vec b=\vec b\cdot\vec b$.
$\vec b\cdot\vec b=9(1+1+1)=27$, so $[\vec a\ \vec c\ \vec b]=27$.
$\vec a\cdot\left((\vec c\times\vec b)-\vec b-\vec c\right)=[\vec a\ \vec c\ \vec b]-\vec a\cdot\vec b-\vec a\cdot\vec c=27-0-3=24$, option (2).

alternate_solutions.idea: Solve for $\vec c$ explicitly with $\vec a\times(\vec a\times\vec c)$, then compute directly.
solution: $\vec a\times(\vec a\times\vec c)=(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec a-|\vec a|^2\vec c=\vec a\times\vec b$, so $\vec c=\frac{3\vec a-\vec a\times\vec b}{6}$ (as $|\vec a|^2=6$).

useful_results: $\vec a\times\vec c=\vec b$ is solvable only if $\vec a\cdot\vec b=0$; then $\vec c=\frac{(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec a-\vec a\times\vec b}{|\vec a|^2}$ (all solutions differ by multiples of $\vec a$, fixed by $\vec a\cdot\vec c$).
A cyclic triple product is unchanged: $[\vec a\ \vec c\ \vec b]=\vec a\cdot(\vec c\times\vec b)=(\vec a\times\vec c)\cdot\vec b$; when $\vec a\times\vec c=\vec b$ this is $|\vec b|^2$.
Dot with the given vector before solving: expressions such as $\vec a\cdot(\dots)$ often collapse using the given products.

concepts: Orthocentre of an equilateral triangle and perpendicular distances from it
questions.question: Let the position vectors of the vertices $A,B$ and $C$ of a triangle be $2\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k$, $\hat i+2\hat j+2\hat k$ and $2\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k$ respectively. Let $\ell_1,\ell_2$ and $\ell_3$ be the lengths of perpendiculars drawn from the orthocentre of the triangle on the sides $AB,BC$ and $CA$ respectively, then $\ell_1^2+\ell_2^2+\ell_3^2$ equals:
questions.key_idea: All three sides equal $\sqrt2$, so the triangle is equilateral and the orthocentre is the centroid, at one third of an altitude from each side.
solution: In an equilateral triangle the orthocentre coincides with the centroid $G$, and each altitude has length $\sqrt{2-\frac12}=\sqrt{\frac32}$.
The perpendicular from $G$ to a side is one third of the altitude: $\ell_1=\frac13\sqrt{\frac32}=\frac{1}{\sqrt6}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The orthocentre of an equilateral triangle is also its incentre, so each $\ell$ equals the inradius $r=\frac{\text{Area}}{s}$.
solution: Inradius $r=\frac{\text{Area}}{s}=\frac{\sqrt3/2}{3\sqrt2/2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt6}$, the distance of the centre from every side.

useful_results: In an equilateral triangle of side $s$, circumcentre, centroid, orthocentre and incentre coincide; the distance of this centre from each side is $\frac{s}{2\sqrt3}=\frac{s\sqrt3}{6}$, and from each vertex $\frac{s}{\sqrt3}$.
Check for equilateral: three equal pairwise distances. Here $s=\sqrt2$ gives $\ell=\frac{\sqrt2}{2\sqrt3}=\frac1{\sqrt6}$.
Inradius $r=\frac{\Delta}{s}$ and $\Delta=\frac12|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}|$ together give a quick vector route to distances from the incentre.

concepts: Angle bisector (length of the bisector) of a triangle in coordinates
questions.question: The position vectors of the vertices $A,B$ and $C$ of a triangle are $2\hat i-3\hat j+3\hat k$, $2\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k$ and $-\hat i+\hat j+3\hat k$ respectively. Let $l$ denote the length of the angle bisector $AD$ of $\angle BAC$ where $D$ is on the line segment $BC$, then $2l^2$ equals:
questions.key_idea: $AB=AC=5$, so the bisector from $A$ meets $BC$ at its midpoint.
solution: By the angle bisector theorem $BD:DC=AB:AC=1:1$, so $D$ is the midpoint of $BC$: $D\left(\frac12,\frac32,3\right)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Since $D$ is the midpoint of $BC$, $AD$ is a median; use Apollonius' theorem instead of coordinates of $D$.

useful_results: Angle bisector theorem: the bisector from $A$ meets $BC$ at $D$ with $BD:DC=AB:AC$, so $\vec d=\frac{AC\cdot\vec b+AB\cdot\vec c}{AB+AC}$.
Length of the bisector from $A$: $AD^2=bc\left[1-\frac{a^2}{(b+c)^2}\right]$; if $b=c$ it reduces to the median/altitude.
Apollonius: median length $m_a^2=\frac{2b^2+2c^2-a^2}{4}$, so $4m_a^2=2b^2+2c^2-a^2$ (here $2l^2=\frac{2\cdot25+2\cdot25-10}{2}=45$).

concepts: Internal angle bisector and section formula (length of the bisector)
questions.question: Let $O$ be the origin and the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ be $2\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k$ and $2\hat i+4\hat j+4\hat k$ respectively. If the internal bisector of $\angle AOB$ meets the line $AB$ at $C$, then the length of $OC$ is:
questions.key_idea: The bisector divides $AB$ in the ratio $OA:OB$, so $C$ comes from the section formula.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the length of an internal angle bisector, $OC^2=bc\left[1-\frac{a^2}{(b+c)^2}\right]$, with no coordinates of $C$.

useful_results: Internal bisector of $\angle AOB$ meets $AB$ at $C=\frac{|OB|\,\vec a+|OA|\,\vec b}{|OA|+|OB|}$ (weights are the opposite side lengths).
Length formula (from Stewart's theorem): $OC^2=OA\cdot OB\left[1-\left(\frac{AB}{OA+OB}\right)^2\right]$.
A neat vector form: $\overrightarrow{OC}$ is parallel to $\hat a+\hat b$ (sum of the unit vectors along $OA$ and $OB$).

concepts: Unit vector with prescribed angles to three vectors (dot product)
questions.question: Let a unit vector $\hat u=x\hat i+y\hat j+z\hat k$ make angles $\frac\pi2,\frac\pi3$ and $\frac{2\pi}3$ with the vectors $\frac1{\sqrt2}\hat i+\frac1{\sqrt2}\hat k$, $\frac1{\sqrt2}\hat j+\frac1{\sqrt2}\hat k$ and $\frac1{\sqrt2}\hat i+\frac1{\sqrt2}\hat j$ respectively. If $\vec v=\frac1{\sqrt2}\hat i+\frac1{\sqrt2}\hat j+\frac1{\sqrt2}\hat k$, then $|\hat u-\vec v|^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The three given vectors are unit vectors, so each angle condition is a linear equation $\hat u\cdot\vec p_i=\cos(\text{angle})$ in $x,y,z$.
solution: Let $\vec p_1=\frac1{\sqrt2}\hat i+\frac1{\sqrt2}\hat k$, $\vec p_2=\frac1{\sqrt2}\hat j+\frac1{\sqrt2}\hat k$, $\vec p_3=\frac1{\sqrt2}\hat i+\frac1{\sqrt2}\hat j$; each has length 1.
Angle $\frac\pi2$ with $\vec p_1$: $\hat u\cdot\vec p_1=0$, so $\frac x{\sqrt2}+\frac z{\sqrt2}=0$, i.e. $x+z=0$ ...(i).
Angle $\frac\pi3$ with $\vec p_2$: $\hat u\cdot\vec p_2=\cos\frac\pi3$, so $\frac y{\sqrt2}+\frac z{\sqrt2}=\frac12$, i.e. $y+z=\frac1{\sqrt2}$ ...(ii).
Angle $\frac{2\pi}3$ with $\vec p_3$: $\hat u\cdot\vec p_3=\cos\frac{2\pi}3$, so $\frac x{\sqrt2}+\frac y{\sqrt2}=-\frac12$, i.e. $x+y=-\frac1{\sqrt2}$ ...(iii).
$\hat u-\vec v=\left(-\frac1{\sqrt2}-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)\hat i+\left(0-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)\hat j+0\,\hat k=-\frac2{\sqrt2}\hat i-\frac1{\sqrt2}\hat j$.
questions.correction_note: Typos in the PDF working: the third condition is printed 'x/sqrt2 + 4/sqrt2 = -1/2' (the '4' is the letter y, as the next line 'x+y = -1/sqrt2' shows) and the vector difference ends with a stray 'kn'. Corrected to y/sqrt2 and removed the stray letter. Results unchanged; the answer (1) is right.

alternate_solutions.idea: Notice $\vec v=\frac12(\vec p_1+\vec p_2+\vec p_3)$, so $\hat u\cdot\vec v$ follows from the three given dot products without solving for $\hat u$.
solution: $\vec p_1+\vec p_2+\vec p_3=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(2,2,2)=\sqrt2(1,1,1)$, hence $\vec v=\frac1{\sqrt2}(1,1,1)=\frac12(\vec p_1+\vec p_2+\vec p_3)$.
$\hat u\cdot\vec v=\frac12(\hat u\cdot\vec p_1+\hat u\cdot\vec p_2+\hat u\cdot\vec p_3)=\frac12\left(0+\frac12-\frac12\right)=0$.
$|\hat u-\vec v|^2=|\hat u|^2+|\vec v|^2-2\,\hat u\cdot\vec v=1+\frac32-0=\frac52$.

useful_results: For a unit vector $\hat u$ and unit vectors $\vec p_i$, the condition 'angle $\theta_i$' is the linear equation $\hat u\cdot\vec p_i=\cos\theta_i$; three independent ones determine $\hat u$ (check $|\hat u|=1$).
$|\vec x-\vec y|^2=|\vec x|^2+|\vec y|^2-2\,\vec x\cdot\vec y$: if the target is a distance, look for a way to get $\vec x\cdot\vec y$ alone.
Recognise combinations: here $\vec p_1+\vec p_2+\vec p_3=2\vec v$, so linear combinations of the given dot products give $\hat u\cdot\vec v$ directly.

concepts: Vector and scalar products: angle between $\vec b$ and a vector built from $\vec a\times\vec b$
questions.question: Let $\vec a=a_1\hat i+a_2\hat j+a_3\hat k$ and $\vec b=b_1\hat i+b_2\hat j+b_3\hat k$ be two vectors such that $|\vec a|=1$, $\vec a\cdot\vec b=2$ and $|\vec b|=4$. If $\vec c=2(\vec a\times\vec b)-3\vec b$, then the angle between $\vec b$ and $\vec c$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $\vec a\times\vec b\perp\vec b$ and $\vec a\times\vec b\perp\vec a$, so the dot products of $\vec c$ with $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ lose the cross term.
solution: Given $|\vec a|=1$, $|\vec b|=4$, $\vec a\cdot\vec b=2$ and $\vec c=2(\vec a\times\vec b)-3\vec b$.
Dot with $\vec a$: $\vec c\cdot\vec a=0-3(\vec a\cdot\vec b)=-6$ ...(1).
Dot with $\vec b$: $\vec b\cdot\vec c=0-3|\vec b|^2=-48$ ...(2).
$|\vec c|^2=4|\vec a\times\vec b|^2+9|\vec b|^2$ (cross terms vanish since $(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot\vec b=0$).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's first line reads 'c.c = 4|a x b| + 9|b|^2': the square on |a x b| is missing (it must be 4|a x b|^2, as the next line |a|^2|b|^2 - (a.b)^2 uses). Restored the square. The PDF also gives c.a = -6 and b.c = -48 without the reason; stated (the cross term is perpendicular to a and b). Answer unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Split $\vec c$ into a component along $\vec b$ and a perpendicular one; the angle follows from a right triangle.
solution: $-3\vec b$ lies along $\vec b$ (opposite direction), of length $3\cdot4=12$.
$2(\vec a\times\vec b)$ is perpendicular to $\vec b$, of length $2\sqrt{|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2}=2\sqrt{12}=4\sqrt3$.
So $\vec c$ makes an angle $\varphi$ with $-\vec b$ where $\tan\varphi=\frac{4\sqrt3}{12}=\frac1{\sqrt3}$, i.e. $\varphi=30^\circ$.
The angle between $\vec b$ and $\vec c$ is $180^\circ-30^\circ=150^\circ$, and $\cos150^\circ=-\frac{\sqrt3}2$.

useful_results: $\vec a\times\vec b$ is perpendicular to both $\vec a$ and $\vec b$, so $(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot\vec a=(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot\vec b=0$; use this to drop cross terms.
Lagrange's identity: $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2$.
If $\vec c=\lambda\vec b+\mu\vec n$ with $\vec n\perp\vec b$, then $\tan(\text{angle with }\vec b)=\frac{|\mu||\vec n|}{|\lambda||\vec b|}$ (and the angle is obtuse if $\lambda<0$).

concepts: Magnitude of a vector expression using $\vec b\times\vec a\perp\vec b$
questions.question: Let $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ be two vectors such that $|\vec b|=1$ and $|\vec b\times\vec a|=2$. Then $\left|(\vec b\times\vec a)-\vec b\right|^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $\vec b\times\vec a\perp\vec b$, so the cross term in the expansion of $|(\vec b\times\vec a)-\vec b|^2$ vanishes.
solution: $|(\vec b\times\vec a)-\vec b|^2=|\vec b\times\vec a|^2+|\vec b|^2-2(\vec b\times\vec a)\cdot\vec b$.
$(\vec b\times\vec a)\cdot\vec b=0$ because $\vec b\times\vec a\perp\vec b$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Choose axes so that $\vec b=\hat k$ (allowed because only lengths and perpendicularity matter).
solution: $\vec b\times\vec a=\hat k\times\vec a=(-a_2,a_1,0)$, and $|\vec b\times\vec a|=2$ gives $a_1^2+a_2^2=4$.
$(\vec b\times\vec a)-\vec b=(-a_2,a_1,-1)$, so its squared length is $a_1^2+a_2^2+1=5$.

useful_results: For perpendicular vectors, $|\vec u\pm\vec v|^2=|\vec u|^2+|\vec v|^2$ (Pythagoras); $\vec b\times\vec a$ is always perpendicular to $\vec b$.
$|\vec b\times\vec a|=|\vec b|\,|\vec a|\sin\theta$ is the distance of the tip of $\vec a$ from the line of $\vec b$ times $|\vec b|$.
Choosing coordinate axes along a given vector is legitimate for any question that uses only dot and cross products and lengths.

concepts: Dot and cross product: $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2$ and $|\vec a|$ from the angle
questions.question: Let $\vec a=\hat i+\alpha\hat j+\beta\hat k$, $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R$. Let a vector $\vec b$ be such that the angle between $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ is $\frac\pi4$ and $|\vec b|^2=6$. If $\vec a\cdot\vec b=3\sqrt2$, then the value of $(\alpha^2+\beta^2)|\vec a\times\vec b|^2$ is:
questions.key_idea: $\vec a\cdot\vec b=|\vec a||\vec b|\cos\frac\pi4$ gives $|\vec a|^2=6$, hence $\alpha^2+\beta^2=5$; then $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2\sin^2\frac\pi4$.

alternate_solutions.idea: At $\theta=\frac\pi4$, $\tan\theta=1$, so $|\vec a\times\vec b|=\vec a\cdot\vec b$ immediately.
solution: $|\vec a\times\vec b|=|\vec a||\vec b|\sin\theta$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec b=|\vec a||\vec b|\cos\theta$, so $|\vec a\times\vec b|=\tan\theta\,(\vec a\cdot\vec b)$.
At $\theta=\frac\pi4$: $|\vec a\times\vec b|=3\sqrt2$, so $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=18$.

useful_results: $|\vec a\times\vec b|=\tan\theta\,(\vec a\cdot\vec b)$; for $\theta=45^\circ$ the dot and cross magnitudes are equal.
$|\vec a\times\vec b|^2+(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2$ (Lagrange's identity).
If $\vec a=\hat i+\alpha\hat j+\beta\hat k$ then $|\vec a|^2=1+\alpha^2+\beta^2$: a condition on $|\vec a|$ fixes $\alpha^2+\beta^2$ without finding $\alpha,\beta$ separately.

concepts: Angle bisector in a triangle and projection of a vector
questions.question: Consider a $\triangle ABC$ where $A(1,3,2)$, $B(-2,8,0)$ and $C(3,6,7)$. If the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ meets the line $BC$ at $D$, then the length of the projection of the vector $\overrightarrow{AD}$ on the vector $\overrightarrow{AC}$ is:
questions.key_idea: $AB=AC=\sqrt{38}$, so $AD$ bisects $\angle A$ and meets $BC$ at its midpoint; the projection is $AD\cos\frac A2$.
solution: Method I. The length of the projection of $\overrightarrow{AD}$ on $\overrightarrow{AC}$ is $AD\cos\frac A2$.
The bisector has length $AD=\frac{2bc}{b+c}\cos\frac A2$, so the projection is $\frac{2bc}{b+c}\cos^2\frac A2$.
Using $\cos^2\frac A2=\frac{1+\cos A}{2}$, the projection is $\frac{2bc}{b+c}\cdot\frac{1+\cos A}{2}$.
Method II. $D$ is the midpoint of $BC$: $D\left(\frac12,7,\frac72\right)$.
$\overrightarrow{AD}=\frac{-\hat i+8\hat j+3\hat k}{2}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}=2\hat i+3\hat j+5\hat k$.
questions.correction_note: In Method II the PDF writes AD = (i - 8j - 3k)/2, which is DA (it has the wrong sign). AD = D - A = (-i + 8j + 3k)/2. The length of the projection takes the modulus of the dot product, so the final value 37/(2 sqrt38) is unchanged. Method I's last value (37/(2 sqrt38)) is printed without the intermediate cos A = -1/38; added.

alternate_solutions.idea: $AB=AC$ makes $\overrightarrow{AD}=\frac12(\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{AC})$; take dot products with $\overrightarrow{AC}$.
solution: $\overrightarrow{AB}=(-3,5,-2)$, $\overrightarrow{AC}=(2,3,5)$, $|\overrightarrow{AB}|=|\overrightarrow{AC}|=\sqrt{38}$, so the bisector is the median: $\overrightarrow{AD}=\frac12(\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{AC})$.

useful_results: If $AB=AC$ then the bisector from $A$ is also the median and the altitude: $\overrightarrow{AD}=\frac12(\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{AC})$.

In general $\overrightarrow{AD}=\frac{c\,\overrightarrow{AC}+b\,\overrightarrow{AB}}{b+c}$ with $b=|AC|$, $c=|AB|$ (weights are the lengths of the other two sides), equivalently $\overrightarrow{AD}\parallel\hat{AB}+\hat{AC}$.
Length of the projection of $\vec u$ on $\vec v$ is $\frac{|\vec u\cdot\vec v|}{|\vec v|}$: the modulus makes the sign of $\vec u$ irrelevant.

concepts: Image of a point in a line and direction cosines of a line
questions.question: Let the image of the point $(1,0,7)$ in the line $\frac x1=\frac{y-1}2=\frac{z-2}3$ be the point $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$. Then which one of the following points lies on the line passing through $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ and making angles $\frac{2\pi}3$ and $\frac{3\pi}4$ with $y$-axis and $z$-axis respectively and an acute angle with $x$-axis?
questions.key_idea: The foot of the perpendicular $M$ gives the image $2M-B$; direction cosines $m,n$ are given and $l$ comes from $l^2+m^2+n^2=1$.
solution: Let $B(1,0,7)$ and let the line pass through $A(0,1,2)$ with direction $\vec P=(1,2,3)$.
The foot of the perpendicular is $M=(\lambda,\,1+2\lambda,\,2+3\lambda)$, so $\overrightarrow{BM}=(\lambda-1,\,2\lambda+1,\,3\lambda-5)$.
The direction cosines are $m=\cos\frac{2\pi}3=-\frac12$, $n=\cos\frac{3\pi}4=-\frac1{\sqrt2}$ and $l$ with $l^2+m^2+n^2=1$.
$l^2=1-\frac14-\frac12=\frac14$, so $l=\pm\frac12$; the angle with the $x$-axis is acute, so $l=+\frac12$.
At $x=3$ the parameter is $2$: $y=6-2=4$, $z=3-2\sqrt2$. The point $(3,4,3-2\sqrt2)$ lies on the line: option (4).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's last line reads (x-1)/(+-1) = (y-6)/1 = (z-3)/sqrt2: it has dropped the minus signs of m and n (the line before shows -1/2 and -1/sqrt2) and keeps '+-' although an acute angle with the x-axis forces l = +1/2. With the PDF's printed line, (3,4,3-2sqrt2) would not lie on it. Corrected to direction (1,-1,-sqrt2). Answer (4) is right.

alternate_solutions.idea: Foot of the perpendicular by the projection formula, then eliminate the options by direction cosines of (option $-$ image).
solution: Foot $M=A+\frac{\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}\vec d=A+\frac{14}{14}\vec d=(1,3,5)$, image $=2M-B=(1,6,3)$.

For an option $X$, the line through the image passes through it only if $X-(1,6,3)$ is proportional to $\left(\frac12,-\frac12,-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)\propto(1,-1,-\sqrt2)$: the $y$-change must be minus the $x$-change.

useful_results: Foot of the perpendicular from $B$ on the line $A+t\vec d$ is $A+\frac{(B-A)\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}\vec d$; image $=2\cdot\text{foot}-B$.

Direction cosines satisfy $l^2+m^2+n^2=1$; a line making angles $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ with the axes has direction $(\cos\alpha,\cos\beta,\cos\gamma)$, and 'acute with the $x$-axis' selects the sign of $l$.
When options are points, test proportionality of (option $-$ known point) with the direction vector instead of solving for the full line.

concepts: Point of intersection of two lines and centroid of a triangle
questions.question: Let $PQR$ be a triangle with $R(-1,4,2)$. Suppose $M(2,1,2)$ is the mid point of $PQ$. The distance of the centroid of $\triangle PQR$ from the point of intersection of the lines $\frac{x-2}0=\frac y2=\frac{z+3}{-1}$ and $\frac{x-1}1=\frac{y+3}{-3}=\frac{z+1}1$ is:
questions.key_idea: The centroid depends only on $R$ and the midpoint $M$: $x_P+x_Q=2x_M$ etc., so $P$ and $Q$ need not be found.
solution: A general point of line 1 is $(2,\,2\lambda,\,-\lambda-3)$; of line 2 is $(\mu+1,\,-3\mu-3,\,\mu-1)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The centroid lies on the median $RM$ and divides it $2:1$ from the vertex $R$.
solution: Intersection of the lines: equate the $x$-coordinates ($2=\mu+1$) to get $\mu=1$; then the point is $(2,-6,0)$ on line 2 and the $y$ and $z$ coordinates agree with line 1 ($\lambda=-3$).

useful_results: Centroid via the median: $G=\frac{\vec r+2\vec m}{3}$ where $M$ is the midpoint of the opposite side $PQ$.
Two lines intersect when one choice of parameters satisfies all three coordinate equations; use two coordinates to solve, the third as a check.
A line with a zero direction ratio (here $\frac{x-2}{0}$) lies in a plane parallel to a coordinate plane ($x=2$), which gives one coordinate for free.

concepts: Points at a given distance on a line and centroid of a triangle
questions.question: Let $P$ and $Q$ be the points on the line $\frac{x+3}8=\frac{y-4}2=\frac{z+1}2$ which are at a distance of 6 units from the point $R(1,2,3)$. If the centroid of the triangle $PQR$ is $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$, then $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$ is:
questions.key_idea: Solving $PR=6$ gives two values of the parameter, which are $P$ and $Q$.
solution: A general point of the line is $P(8\lambda-3,\,2\lambda+4,\,2\lambda-1)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: $P,Q$ are symmetric about the foot $N$ of the perpendicular from $R$, so $G=\frac{2N+R}{3}$ and only $N$ is needed.
solution: The midpoint $N$ of $PQ$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $R$ (equal distances 6 from $R$).

useful_results: Two points of a line at equal distance from an external point $R$ are symmetric about the foot of the perpendicular from $R$; the midpoint of $PQ$ is that foot.
Centroid of $PQR$ $=\frac{2N+R}{3}$ with $N$ the midpoint of $PQ$.

A point on $\frac{x-x_0}{a}=\dots$ at distance $d$ from $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ has parameter $t=\pm\frac{d}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}$ if written as $(x_0+at,\dots)$; here the distance condition from $R$ is a quadratic in $\lambda$ whose two roots are $P$ and $Q$.

concepts: Vector product equation $\vec b\times\vec d=\vec c\times\vec d$ and Lagrange's identity
questions.question: Let $\vec a=\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k$, $\vec b=3\hat i-3\hat j+3\hat k$, $\vec c=2\hat i-\hat j+2\hat k$ and $\vec d$ be a vector such that $\vec b\times\vec d=\vec c\times\vec d$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec d=4$. Then $\left|\vec a\times\vec d\right|^2$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: $(\vec b-\vec c)\times\vec d=\vec 0$ means $\vec d$ is parallel to $\vec b-\vec c$; the dot product with $\vec a$ then fixes the scalar.
solution: $\vec b\times\vec d=\vec c\times\vec d$ gives $(\vec b-\vec c)\times\vec d=\vec 0$.
Hence $\vec b-\vec c=\lambda\vec d$ for some scalar $\lambda$.
Dot with $\vec a$: $\vec a\cdot\vec b-\vec a\cdot\vec c=\lambda\,\vec a\cdot\vec d$, i.e. $0-2=4\lambda$, so $\lambda=-\frac12$.
$\vec b=\vec c+\lambda\vec d$ gives $\vec d=\frac{\vec b-\vec c}{\lambda}=2(\vec c-\vec b)=2(-\hat i+2\hat j-\hat k)$.
$|\vec a\times\vec d|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec d|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec d)^2=6\times24-16=16(9-1)=128$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes d = 2(c-b) = 2(-i + 2j + k). But c - b = (2-3, -1+3, 2-3) = (-1, 2, -1), so d = 2(-i + 2j - k) = (-2, 4, -2); with +k the condition a.d = 4 would fail (it would give 8). |d|^2 = 24 is the same either way, so the answer 128 is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $\vec d=\mu(\vec c-\vec b)$ from the start and compute $\vec a\times\vec d$ by a direct cross product.
solution: $(\vec b-\vec c)\times\vec d=\vec 0$ means $\vec d\parallel\vec c-\vec b=(-1,2,-1)$, so $\vec d=\mu(-1,2,-1)$.

useful_results: $\vec u\times\vec d=\vec v\times\vec d\iff(\vec u-\vec v)\parallel\vec d$ (when $\vec d\ne\vec 0$): a cross-product equation with the same factor on both sides says the difference is parallel to that factor.
Lagrange: $|\vec a\times\vec d|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec d|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec d)^2$ avoids computing the cross product when the dot product is known.
Dotting a vector equation with a suitable vector (here $\vec a$, which is perpendicular to $\vec b$) usually eliminates unknowns quickly.

concepts: Centroid of a triangle and sum of squares of distances (vector form)
questions.question: Let the three sides of a triangle $ABC$ be given by the vectors $2\hat i-\hat j+\hat k$, $\hat i-3\hat j-5\hat k$ and $3\hat i-4\hat j-4\hat k$. Let $G$ be the centroid of the triangle $ABC$. Then $6\left(|\overrightarrow{AG}|^2+|\overrightarrow{BG}|^2+|\overrightarrow{CG}|^2\right)$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: Putting $A$ at the origin turns the side vectors into the position vectors of $B$ and $C$, and $G$ is the average of the three vertices.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $GA^2+GB^2+GC^2=\frac13\left(a^2+b^2+c^2\right)$ in terms of the squares of the three side lengths.
solution: Sum of squares of the sides $=6+35+41=82$.

useful_results: For a triangle with centroid $G$: $GA^2+GB^2+GC^2=\frac13\left(AB^2+BC^2+CA^2\right)$ (Leibniz/Lagrange relation).
For any point $P$: $PA^2+PB^2+PC^2=GA^2+GB^2+GC^2+3PG^2$; the sum is least at $P=G$.

Three side vectors of a closed triangle sum to zero as $\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{BC}+\overrightarrow{CA}=\vec 0$; here the data satisfy $\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{BC}=\overrightarrow{AC}$, which gives a quick consistency check.

concepts: Vertices of a triangle formed by three lines and its area (cross product)
questions.question: Let the area of the triangle formed by the lines $x+2=y-1=z$, $\frac{x-3}5=\frac y{-1}=\frac{z-1}1$ and $\frac x{-3}=\frac{y-3}3=\frac{z-2}1$ be $A$. Then $A^2$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: Intersect the lines in pairs to get the three vertices, then use $\frac12|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}|$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF labels the vertex A as (-1, 1, 0). The lines x+2 = y-1 = z and (x-3)/5 = y/(-1) = (z-1)/1 meet at (-2, 1, 0) (t = 0, s = -1), not (-1, 1, 0). The vectors AB = (5,-1,1), AC = (2,2,2) used afterwards are those of (-2,1,0) to B(3,0,1) and C(0,3,2), so the area and the answer 56 are right; only the printed coordinates of A were wrong. Also the PDF stops at A = sqrt(4+16+36); the step A^2 = 56 was added.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use Lagrange's identity $|\vec u\times\vec v|^2=|\vec u|^2|\vec v|^2-(\vec u\cdot\vec v)^2$ to skip the determinant.

useful_results: Area of a triangle with sides $\vec u,\vec v$: $A^2=\frac14\left(|\vec u|^2|\vec v|^2-(\vec u\cdot\vec v)^2\right)$; no determinant needed.
Three coplanar lines pairwise meeting (not concurrent) form a triangle: find each vertex from a pair of lines; a quick check is that all three lines lie in one plane.
Parameter-matching method: for lines $\vec p+t\vec d$ and $\vec q+s\vec e$, equate two coordinates to solve for $t,s$, and confirm with the third.

concepts: Projection of a vector and area of a parallelogram
questions.question: Let $\vec c$ be the projection vector of $\vec b=\lambda\hat i+4\hat k$, $\lambda>0$, on the vector $\vec a=\hat i+2\hat j+2\hat k$. If $|\vec a+\vec c|=7$, then the area of the parallelogram formed by the vectors $\vec b$ and $\vec c$ is ________.
questions.key_idea: $\vec c$ is parallel to $\vec a$, so $|\vec a+\vec c|=7$ gives $\lambda$; the area is then $|\vec b\times\vec c|$.
solution: $\vec c=\left(\frac{\vec b\cdot\vec a}{|\vec a|}\right)\frac{\vec a}{|\vec a|}=\frac{\vec b\cdot\vec a}{|\vec a|^2}\vec a=\frac{\lambda+8}{9}\left(\hat i+2\hat j+2\hat k\right)$.
$\vec a+\vec c=\left(1+\frac{\lambda+8}9\right)\vec a$, so $|\vec a+\vec c|=3\left(1+\frac{\lambda+8}9\right)=7$.
Area $=|\vec b\times\vec c|=|\vec c\times\vec b|$ and $\vec c\times\vec b=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\\frac43&\frac83&\frac83\\4&0&4\end{matrix}\right|$.
questions.correction_note: Two points in the PDF: (1) the line '|a + c| - = 7 => lambda = 4' has a stray dash and skips the equation 3(1 + (lambda+8)/9) = 7; added. (2) The determinant is printed with rows c then b and the result is given as 16 with no components; rows c, b give c x b, whose magnitude equals |b x c|. The explicit cross product (32/3, 16/3, -32/3) was added. Answer 16 unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Since $\vec b=\vec c+\vec b_\perp$ with $\vec b_\perp\perp\vec c$, the parallelogram area is $|\vec c|\,|\vec b_\perp|$.
solution: $\vec c\parallel\vec a$ in the same direction ($\vec b\cdot\vec a=\lambda+8>0$), so $|\vec a+\vec c|=|\vec a|+|\vec c|=3+|\vec c|=7$, giving $|\vec c|=4$.
$\vec b=\vec c+\vec b_\perp$ with $\vec b_\perp\perp\vec c$, so $|\vec b_\perp|^2=32-16=16$.
$\vec b\times\vec c=\vec b_\perp\times\vec c$ has magnitude $|\vec b_\perp||\vec c|=4\times4=16$.

useful_results: Projection vector of $\vec b$ on $\vec a$: $\frac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{|\vec a|^2}\vec a$; the scalar projection is $\frac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{|\vec a|}$.

$|\vec b|^2=|\vec b_\parallel|^2+|\vec b_\perp|^2$ and the area of the parallelogram on $\vec b$ and a vector $\vec c\parallel\vec a$ is $|\vec c|\,|\vec b_\perp|$ (component of $\vec b$ perpendicular to $\vec c$).
If $\vec c\parallel\vec a$ in the same direction, $|\vec a+\vec c|=|\vec a|+|\vec c|$.

concepts: Vector triple product and magnitude of a cross product with given angle
questions.question: Let $\vec a=\hat i+\hat j+\hat k$, $\vec b=2\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k$ and $\vec d=\vec a\times\vec b$. If $\vec c$ is a vector such that $\vec a\cdot\vec c=|\vec c|$, $|\vec c-2\vec a|^2=8$ and the angle between $\vec d$ and $\vec c$ is $\frac\pi4$, then $|10-3\vec b\cdot\vec c|+|\vec d\times\vec c|^2$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: $|\vec c-2\vec a|^2=8$ with $\vec a\cdot\vec c=|\vec c|$ gives $|\vec c|=2$; expanding $\vec d\times\vec c=(\vec a\times\vec b)\times\vec c$ gives $\vec b\cdot\vec c$.
solution: $\vec d=\vec a\times\vec b=-\hat i+\hat j$, so $|\vec d|=\sqrt2$.
$|\vec c-2\vec a|^2=8$: $|\vec c|^2+4|\vec a|^2-4(\vec a\cdot\vec c)=8$.
With $|\vec a|^2=3$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec c=|\vec c|$: $|\vec c|^2+12-4|\vec c|=8$, i.e. $|\vec c|^2-4|\vec c|+4=0$, so $|\vec c|=2$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec c=2$.
$\vec d\times\vec c=(\vec a\times\vec b)\times\vec c=(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec b-(\vec b\cdot\vec c)\vec a$.

Squared magnitudes: $|\vec d\times\vec c|^2=\left(|\vec d||\vec c|\sin\frac\pi4\right)^2=4$ on the left, and on the right $(\vec a\cdot\vec c)^2|\vec b|^2+(\vec b\cdot\vec c)^2|\vec a|^2-2(\vec a\cdot\vec c)(\vec b\cdot\vec c)(\vec a\cdot\vec b)$.
With $|\vec b|^2=9$, $|\vec a|^2=3$, $\vec a\cdot\vec b=5$ and $x=\vec b\cdot\vec c$: $4=36+3x^2-20x$, i.e. $3x^2-20x+32=0$.
$|\vec d\times\vec c|^2=4$ and $|10-3\vec b\cdot\vec c|=|10-8|=2$ or $|10-12|=2$; either way the sum is $2+4=6$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's line '(|a||c| sin(pi/4))^2 = ((a.c) b - (b.c) a)^2' uses |a| where it must be |d| = |a x b| = sqrt2 (the angle pi/4 is between d and c): (|d||c| sin(pi/4))^2 = (sqrt2*2*(1/sqrt2))^2 = 4, which is the '4' written on the left. With |a| = sqrt3 the left side would be 6. Also the PDF shows only the quadratic and not a.b = 5, |a|^2 = 3, |b|^2 = 9, and writes the final sum as '|10-8| + (2)^2'. Corrected |a| to |d| and spelled out the constants; the answer 6 is right and holds for both roots.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find $\vec c$ itself: $\vec a\cdot\vec c=2$, $\vec d\cdot\vec c=2$ and $|\vec c|=2$ determine it.
solution: As before $|\vec c|=2$, $\vec a\cdot\vec c=2$; $\vec d=(-1,1,0)$ with $\vec d\cdot\vec c=|\vec d||\vec c|\cos\frac\pi4=\sqrt2\cdot2\cdot\frac1{\sqrt2}=2$.
$\vec c=(0,2,0)$ or $\left(-\frac23,\frac43,\frac43\right)$; then $\vec b\cdot\vec c=4$ or $-\frac43+\frac83+\frac43=\frac83$.
$|10-3\vec b\cdot\vec c|=2$ in both cases, and $|\vec d\times\vec c|^2=|\vec d|^2|\vec c|^2\sin^2\frac\pi4=2\cdot4\cdot\frac12=4$.

useful_results: Vector triple product: $(\vec a\times\vec b)\times\vec c=(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec b-(\vec b\cdot\vec c)\vec a$ (the result lies in the plane of $\vec a,\vec b$).
$|\vec u-k\vec a|^2=|\vec u|^2+k^2|\vec a|^2-2k\,\vec u\cdot\vec a$; with $\vec a\cdot\vec c=|\vec c|$ it becomes a quadratic in $|\vec c|$, here a perfect square.

$|\vec d\times\vec c|^2=|\vec d|^2|\vec c|^2-(\vec d\cdot\vec c)^2$: with the angle between $\vec d$ and $\vec c$ known and their lengths known this is immediate, without the triple-product expansion.

concepts: Consistency of a system of linear equations (determinant zero)
Sum of powers $\sum n$ and $\sum n^2$
questions.question: Let $\alpha,\beta\,(\alpha\neq\beta)$ be the values of $m$, for which the equations $x+y+z=1$; $x+2y+4z=m$ and $x+4y+10z=m^2$ have infinitely many solutions. Then the value of $\sum\limits_{n=1}^{10}\left(n^\alpha+n^\beta\right)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The coefficient determinant is 0, so the system is consistent only when the right-hand sides obey the same row dependency.
solution: For infinitely many solutions $\Delta_x=\Delta_y=\Delta_z=0$ must also hold.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes the condition as 'm^2 - 3x + 2 = 0' (the letter x instead of m). Corrected to m^2 - 3m + 2 = 0. Answer 440 unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Notice the third equation's row is $3R_2-2R_1$; consistency needs the same combination of right-hand sides.
solution: Forming $R_3-3R_2+2R_1$ gives $0=m^2-3m+2$ on the right-hand side.
For infinitely many solutions this must be $0=0$: $(m-1)(m-2)=0$, $m=1,2$. For these values $R_1,R_2$ are independent, so there is a one-parameter family.

useful_results: If one row of the coefficient matrix is a combination of the others, the system is consistent only if the same combination holds for the constants; then the solutions form a line (one free parameter) when the rank is 2.
$\Delta=0$ alone gives no solution or infinitely many; checking one numerator determinant (or the row-combination identity) decides.
